summary:
The Konya Plain pumps more groundwater than it can sustain, so an irrigation cooperative must decide each season which member grows what, on how much land and with how much water, while still
  delivering the tonnage promised to buyers. Nobet does not tell the farmer what to plant. It turns that choice into a water budget and shows what each option costs.
  It starts from NASA POWER daily data for each district, October 2004 to December 2025: temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, wind, humidity and elevation. Daily reference evapotranspiration
  comes from the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation. A soil-water bucket applies crop coefficients by growth stage, rainfall, a shared quota and irrigation efficiency, and season-long stress becomes
  relative yield through FAO-33 coefficients. Every option is replayed on the twenty real seasons from 2006 to 2025, giving a spread of outcomes instead of one average year.
  
  A linear program then splits each member's land across crops and water levels, reserving water at each option's driest year so a plan never exceeds the quota. It maximises revenue or minimises
  water while meeting deliveries, under real cooperative rules: no crop on more than a third of a field, a minimum parcel size, and irrigated crops at no less than 60 percent of full demand. If a
  promise cannot be met, it returns the best achievable share and the cost of closing the gap.
details:
The decision this project is built for

An irrigation cooperative on the Konya Plain has a fixed seasonal water quota and a tonnage it has promised to a buyer. It has to say which member grows which crop, on how many decares, and with

how much water. Guessing is expensive in both directions: over-promise and the delivery fails in a dry year; under-water a crop and the yield collapses while the quota is already spent. Nöbet is a

water-budget planner for that decision. It does not recommend a crop. It prices the options.

Where the numbers come from

The climate is not invented. For each district the tool uses NASA POWER daily data from 1 October 2004 to 31 December 2025: maximum and minimum temperature, corrected precipitation, all-sky

surface shortwave radiation, wind at 2 m, relative humidity, and elevation. Daily reference evapotranspiration is computed with the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith equation. A one-layer soil-water bucket

then walks every day of a season — crop coefficient by growth stage, rain, a shared quota, irrigation efficiency — and turns the resulting water stress into relative yield with FAO-33

yield-response coefficients. Each option is replayed on the twenty real seasons from 2006 to 2025. A linear program then assigns every member's land to crop-and-water-level pairs, reserving water

at each option's worst year, so a plan that fits on paper also fits in the driest year of the record.

Three problems, worked on Karapınar's own record

The July gap. In Karapınar, July rainfall averages 4.3 mm and stays under 9 mm in 19 of the 20 seasons (2009, at 26 mm, is the exception). July reference evapotranspiration over the same years

averages 215 mm, ranging from 190 to 231. Annual evapotranspiration averages 1,241 mm. A summer crop is not short of a few irrigations. It is short of almost the entire month.

A quota that looks generous and runs out anyway. Give the whole field to maize and cap the season at 200 mm. On this climate the water is finished between 7 and 24 July with sprinkler or drip

irrigation, and in 19 of 20 years inside the first three weeks of July. Flood irrigation, at half the efficiency, finishes between 27 June and 15 July. The same record says what "no irrigation"

actually returns: rainfed maize averages 5 percent of a fully watered yield, and never better than 16 percent. Rainfed winter wheat averages 53 percent. Fully watered maize, at 80 percent

irrigation efficiency, needs about 801 mm gross — four times the 200 mm quota. The quota is not a yield target. It is a ration, and the ration decides the crop.

The same promise, three ways of keeping it. The sample cooperative — fifty fictional members across Karapınar, Çumra, Ereğli, Cihanbeyli and Altınekin, each calculated on that district's NASA cell

— is given one maize delivery and three ways to spread it. Today's planting holds the promise in 2 of 20 seasons. Assigning whole fields at random until the tonnage is covered holds it in 8. The

planned allocation, which splits fields and caps each parcel's water at its driest year, holds it in 16. The tool's "safe amount" is defined the same way: the largest tonnage the plan still

delivers in at least 16 of the 20 historical seasons. A promise written above that line is not a plan. It is a bet on a wet year.

What the cooperative sees, and what the tool refuses to do

The opening screen puts the three distributions side by side on the same six measures: members growing the crop, average yield, years the promise holds, water used, gross income, and members who

run out of water mid-season. If the promised tonnage cannot be grown under the rules, the solver does not return a blank page. It returns the largest share of the promise that can be met, and the

cost of three remedies — lower the promise, relax the one-third cap on a single crop, or raise the quotas. Rules a cooperative actually uses are constraints, not advice: no crop on more than a

third of a field, a crop planted on at least 10 decares or not at all (5 on farms under 60), an irrigated crop receiving at least 60 percent of its full demand or dropped, and sugar beet offered

only to a contracted member and only at full irrigation, because it is the thirstiest crop in the set and a single seasonal yield coefficient is not trustworthy when that crop is kept short of

water.

Equally deliberate is what is labelled as an assumption rather than a measurement. Crop coefficients, full-irrigation yields and prices are editable and marked unverified wherever they were not

read off a cited table. Income is gross. NASA POWER describes a district at roughly 55 km, not a field, so local hail, frost pockets and a single storm do not appear. The yield response is one

coefficient for the whole season, not stage by stage. Prices do not move, and twenty years of weather are not a forecast. The screen says so. The point of the project is that a cooperative can see

those limits and still get a water budget it can defend — one that was run on the years that already happened, not on an average year that never did.
